beats.say: Week five. Managing the evolution of brands, with Shannon Wright, Head of Marketing for Confectionery at Nestlé Oceania. She leads KitKat and Allen's.

board.title: Managing the **evolution** of brands
board.name: Shannon Wright
board.org: Head of Marketing, Confectionery, Nestlé Oceania

beats.say: First, career advice. Be interested in the unfamiliar, know what matters to you, stay curious, and be a good person. The industry is small.
Two brands, opposite problems. KitKat takes the consistency path. Allen's must define its long-term path as trends shift underneath it.
KitKat stands for a break. It was made for workers on their break, and the bar takes two hands to snap, so you stop.
Three truths line up. Brand belief: breaks are good. Audience truth: everyone needs one. Product truth: it's made to be broken.
The most dangerous person in marketing is the bored brand manager, who changes things that didn't need changing. Have a strategy.
Consistency is a superpower. The need hasn't changed, but the tension has. Sixty three percent of Gen Z need a break, yet sixty four percent can't switch off.
They sit down, doom scroll, and their minds stay busy. So KitKat's job now is the emotional break, not just the physical one.
Distinctive brand assets shortcut people to you: the bar, the red, the snap. Use them or lose them. Even Have a, unfinished, works, because your brain closes the gap.
The second most dangerous person is the brand manager with no ambition. Cultural relevance is a currency. Impact comes from brand size, creative quality and budget setting.
Fans argued over the right way to eat a KitKat: around twenty seven million social engagements. A debate about your brand is a jackpot, so fan the flames.
Four principles. Meet your audience where they are. Tone and timing are everything. Be clear on the brand's role. And subvert your equity to be one of the people.
Now Allen's. People love it, but a brand is a leaky bucket that drains unless you refill it. We want a playground, not a museum.
Gen Z want intense flavours and surprising textures. Forty five percent of Australians say texture appeals, and lolly salads turn sweets into social currency.
GLP-1 drugs could reach fifteen percent of Australians by year end, dulling the joy of sweets. And India has overtaken England for migration, bringing new tastes.
When Arnott's changed four Shapes flavours, people were outraged. A heritage brand doesn't have to taste better. It has to taste the same.
Know your consumers, potential consumers and brand. Then test any stretch for fit, distance from the core, consumer permission, risk versus reward, and keep monitoring.
For Heinz, soup is a near step, pasta sauce a credible stretch, vodka the exception. Or collaborate, like Allen's with Pepsi and Mountain Dew.
So: protect your assets, and know why you're entering culture. Know your consumers and who you are. Use AI to ease the work, not do the thinking. That's week five.
